title: The likelihood: the same formula read as a function of the parameter

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The binomial formula of section 12 gives the probability of k successes in n independent trials. Each trial has the same probability of a success, p.

P(X = k) = (n choose k) × pk × (1 − p)(n − k)

The count k is the data, already observed, and p is the unknown parameter.

Keep k and n fixed at the data, and let p vary. Read this way, the same expression is the likelihood of p, written L(p) and read “the likelihood of p”.

L(p) = (n choose k) × pk × (1 − p)(n − k), with k and n fixed at the data

L(p) is the probability of the data you got, if the parameter were p. It is not the probability that the parameter is p.

The term pk × (1 − p)(n − k) is the probability of one particular order of k successes and n − k failures. It is a product because the trials are independent (section 3): the probability of all the observations together is the product of their separate probabilities. Without independence, the likelihood is not a product, and this formula is wrong.

Divide the likelihoods of two values of p, L(p1) ÷ L(p2). The result is the likelihood ratio of section 8. Its two hypotheses are “p = p1” and “p = p2”, and the data are the evidence. It says how many times more probable the data are under p1 than under p2. The factor n choose k is the same for every p, so it cancels from every ratio.

The value of p with the largest likelihood is the best-supported value, called the maximum likelihood estimate. For a binomial count it is k ÷ n, the sample share p̂ of section 19. That this holds for every n and k is shown in the next rung.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
You know how to ask: if the true share were 0.3, how likely is it that 3 of 10 people have the feature?

Now turn it round. You have seen 3 of 10. Try one possible share after another, and ask the same question each time. The answers form the likelihood.

The likelihood is a probability of the data. It is never the probability that a share is true.

blocks.alt: Points at p = 0.1 to 0.9 rising from 0.0574 to a peak of 0.2668 at 0.3, then falling to 0.1172 at 0.5, 0.0008 at 0.8 and 0.00001 at 0.9, with a smooth curve through them and a dashed line at 0.3.
blocks.caption: The likelihood of the share p after 3 of 10 women had a body-mass index of 25 or more (made-up data), L(p) = 120 × p<sup>3</sup> × (1 − p)<sup>7</sup>. The curve is highest at p = 0.3, the sample share. Each point is the probability of the same data under a different p, so the points are not a distribution for p.

blocks.alt: A narrow peaked curve from p = 0.2 to 0.6, at 1 at p = 0.397 and almost flat on the axis at 0.2 and 0.6, with points at 0.3 and 0.5 both at about 0.06.
blocks.caption: The likelihood of the share p after 52 of 131 men had a body-mass index of 25 or more, as a fraction of its peak at 0.397, the sample share. At 0.30 and at 0.50 it is about 0.06 of the peak, so their ratio is about 1.02 and the data barely tell them apart, though both are far below the peak. At 0.20 it is about 1 in 609,000 of the peak.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Here is a made-up result. At a screening camp, 3 of 10 women measured have a body-mass index of 25 kg/m2 or more. Treat the 10 as independent trials with an unknown share p. You want to know which values of p the data support.

First the fixed part. The number of orders of 3 successes among 10 is 10 choose 3 (section 11).

10 choose 3 = 10! ÷ (3! × 7!) = (10 × 9 × 8) ÷ (3 × 2 × 1) = 720 ÷ 6 = 120

So L(p) = 120 × p3 × (1 − p)7. Work it out at p = 0.3.

0.33 = 0.027
0.77 = 0.0823543
120 times 0.027 times 0.0823543 = 0.2668

Do the same at each tenth from 0.1 to 0.9.

p L(p)
0.1 0.0574
0.2 0.2013
0.3 0.2668
0.4 0.2150
0.5 0.1172
0.6 0.0425
0.7 0.0090
0.8 0.0008
0.9 0.00001

The largest likelihood in the table is at p = 0.3, which is 3 ÷ 10, the sample share.

Now add the column.

0.0574 plus 0.2013 plus 0.2668 plus 0.2150 plus 0.1172 = 0.8577
0.0425 plus 0.0090 plus 0.0008 plus 0.00001 = 0.05231
0.8577 plus 0.05231 = 0.91001

About 0.91, not 1. Try p = 0.25 and p = 0.35 as well and the total grows past 1. These are not the probabilities of nine possible values of p. Each one is the probability of the same data under a different p.

Compare two values by dividing. The 120 cancels.

0.2668 divided by 0.1172 = 2.28
0.2668 divided by 0.0574 = 4.65

The data are about 2.3 times as probable if p is 0.3 as if p is 0.5. They are about 4.6 times as probable if p is 0.3 as if p is 0.1. That is all the likelihood says. It does not say how probable 0.3 is.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The camp and its count are made up. The likelihood is only as good as the binomial model behind it: independent women, one shared p. Women from the same household or the same lane share food, work and income, and their results are tied (section 3). Then the product is wrong, and the likelihood comes out more sharply peaked than the data justify.

The table steps in tenths. The best-supported value happens to fall on a tenth here; in general it sits between the rows, at k ÷ n.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now real counts. Kiran and colleagues measured 131 male medical students at one college. Open their paper in Heliyon at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9791811/. Table 2 puts 42 men in the body-mass index band 25 to 29.9 kg/m2 and 10 at 30 or more. So 52 of 131 had an index of 25 or more. The best-supported p is the sample share.

52 divided by 131 is about 0.397

The authors planned their sample size on a share of 20 per cent, taken from the fourth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-4). How much better do the data support 0.397 than 0.20?

Dividing two powers with the same exponent gives the power of the quotient: 62 ÷ 32 = 36 ÷ 9 = 4 = 22. So the ratio is (0.397 ÷ 0.20)52 × (0.603 ÷ 0.80)79, because 131 minus 52 is 79 and 1 minus 0.397 is 0.603. The powers are too large for a pocket calculator to show cleanly, so work in log10. A logarithm turns multiplication into addition (Book 0, A7). A power is repeated multiplication, so its log is the power times the log. Check: 23 = 8, and 3 × 0.30103 = 0.90309, which is log10 of 8.

0.397 divided by 0.2 = 1.985
0.603 divided by 0.8 = 0.75375
52 times 0.29776 = 15.4835
79 times -0.12277 = -9.6988
15.4835 plus -9.6988 = 5.7847

Here 0.29776 is log10 of 1.985, and −0.12277 is log10 of 0.75375. The ratio is 105.7847, about 609,000. The data are hundreds of thousands of times more probable if the share among the population these men stand for is 0.397 than if it is 0.20.

Now compare 0.30 with 0.50, two values on either side of the peak.

0.3 divided by 0.5 = 0.6
0.7 divided by 0.5 = 1.4
52 times -0.22185 = -11.5362
79 times 0.14613 = 11.5443
-11.5362 plus 11.5443 = 0.0081

The ratio is 100.0081, about 1.02. The data barely tell 0.30 from 0.50. That does not mean the data are vague. Both values are far below the peak: each has a likelihood about 0.06 times that of 0.397 (practice problem 6 works this out). A ratio of two values tells you only about those two.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The 131 men volunteered at one college. A likelihood built on them describes the share in a population that resembles them, not the share in young Indian men, and it assumes the men’s results are independent of one another.

The 0.20 was a planning figure for a sample size, not a measured share in this college. The huge ratio shows that the college’s men did not look like 0.20. It does not show that 0.20 was wrong for the population NFHS-4 described.

The logs are rounded to five figures, which is enough for a ratio quoted to two or three.

points.html: “The likelihood of p = 0.3 is 0.27, so there is a 27 per cent chance the share is 0.3” is the error. It reads P(data | p) as P(p | data), the transposed conditional of section 9. A likelihood is the probability of the data if p were 0.3. A probability that p is 0.3 needs a prior for p, as a diagnosis did in section 5. That is a later book’s subject.
A small likelihood under one value means nothing until you set it beside the likelihood under a rival value.
The likelihood multiplies the probabilities of the separate observations, which is right only if they are independent.
A likelihood ratio near 1 between two values says only that the data do not separate those two.
When a paper reports a “maximum likelihood estimate” of a simple proportion, check it against k ÷ n.
Teach the likelihood as the binomial formula read sideways: the same expression, with the data held fixed and p moving.

blocks.label: Common misreading
blocks.html: “The likelihood is highest at 0.397, so 0.397 is probably the true share.” The likelihood ranks values of p by how well they predict the data you got. It puts no probability on any value being true; that would need a prior, as a diagnosis does. Say “the data are best supported by a share of about 0.4”, and give the ratio to any rival value you mean to discuss.

blocks.prompt: From memory: what is the likelihood of a parameter value? Why do likelihoods across p not have to add to 1? What does the ratio of two likelihoods tell you?
blocks.answer:
The likelihood of a value of p is the probability of the observed data if the parameter were that value. The data are held fixed and p is varied.

Each is a probability of the same data under a different p. None is the probability of a p, and nothing in the model makes p a random variable. So they need not add to 1.

The ratio L(p1) ÷ L(p2) says how many times more probable the data are under p1 than under p2. It is the likelihood ratio of the odds form of Bayes’ theorem. The two values of p are its two hypotheses.

blocks.prompt:
A results section says this.

The maximum likelihood estimate of the prevalence was 0.397. The likelihood at the national figure of 0.273 was less than 1 in 100 of the maximum, so the national prevalence is excluded.

The data are Kiran’s 52 of 131 men. Check the ratio, and say what the sentence shows and what “excluded” overstates.
blocks.answer:
The ratio of the maximum to the likelihood at 0.273 is (0.397 ÷ 0.273)52 × (0.603 ÷ 0.727)79.

0.397 divided by 0.273 = 1.45421
0.603 divided by 0.727 = 0.82944
log10 1.45421 = 0.16263
log10 0.82944 = -0.08122
52 times 0.16263 = 8.4568
79 times -0.08122 = -6.4164
8.4568 plus -6.4164 = 2.0404

102.0404 is about 110. So the likelihood at 0.273 is about 1 in 110 of the maximum, and the sentence’s “less than 1 in 100” is right.

What it shows: these 131 men’s counts are far more probable under a share near 0.4 than under 0.273.

What “excluded” overstates. A likelihood ratio does not exclude a value; turning it into a decision needs a rule the next rung teaches. And the comparison is of different populations. The 0.273 is the 27.3 per cent of NFHS-6, 2023-24, for men aged 15 to 49 across India. The 0.397 is for male medical students who volunteered at one college. Nothing here says the national figure is wrong for the nation.

blocks.prompt: In 3 independent trials there were 2 successes. Work out L(p) at p = 0.5 and at p = 0.6. Which value do the data support better?
blocks.answer:
L(p) = (3 choose 2) × p2 × (1 − p). 3 choose 2 is 3.

3 times 0.25 times 0.5 = 0.375
3 times 0.36 times 0.4 = 0.432

L(0.5) = 0.375 and L(0.6) = 0.432. The data support 0.6 better.

blocks.prompt: In 10 independent trials there were 6 successes. Work out the likelihood ratio L(0.6) ÷ L(0.4) without working out 10 choose 6.
blocks.answer:
The factor 10 choose 6 is in both likelihoods, so it cancels.

0.6 divided by 0.4 = 1.5
0.4 divided by 0.6 = 0.6667
1.56 = 11.390625
0.66674 = 0.19757
11.390625 times 0.19757 = 2.25

The data are 2.25 times as probable if p is 0.6 as if p is 0.4.

blocks.prompt: In 4 independent trials there was 1 success. Work out L(p) at p = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8, and say which is best supported. Then work out L at the sample share.
blocks.answer:
L(p) = 4 × p × (1 − p)3.

4 times 0.2 times 0.512 = 0.4096
4 times 0.4 times 0.216 = 0.3456
4 times 0.6 times 0.064 = 0.1536
4 times 0.8 times 0.008 = 0.0256

Of the four, 0.2 is best supported. The sample share is 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25.

4 times 0.25 times 0.421875 = 0.421875

L(0.25) is about 0.4219, higher than any of the four.

blocks.prompt:
In Kiran and colleagues’ Table 2, 46 of 151 women had a body-mass index of 25 or more. Of them, 41 were in the band 25 to 29.9 and 5 were at 30 or more. NFHS-6 gives 30.7 per cent for women aged 15 to 49 in India.

Work out the best-supported share for the population these women stand for. Then work out how many times more probable the counts are at that share than at 0.307, using log10. Say what the ratio does and does not show.
blocks.answer:
46 divided by 151 is about 0.305
151 minus 46 = 105
1 minus 0.305 = 0.695
1 minus 0.307 = 0.693
0.305 divided by 0.307 = 0.993485
0.695 divided by 0.693 = 1.002886
46 times -0.0028387 = -0.13058
105 times 0.0012516 = 0.13142
-0.13058 plus 0.13142 = 0.00084

Here −0.0028387 is log10 of 0.993485, and 0.0012516 is log10 of 1.002886. The ratio is 100.00084, about 1.002.

The best-supported share is 0.305. The counts are almost exactly as probable at 0.307.

What it shows: these 151 women’s counts fit 0.305 and 0.307 about equally. What it does not show: that these women stand for young Indian women. They are volunteer medical students at one college. A ratio near 1 says the data do not separate two values; it does not say the two groups are the same.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer about 3 successes in 10 trials. Find the step that broke.

L(0.3) = 120 times 0.33 times 0.77 = 0.2668
so the probability that p = 0.3 is 0.2668
so there is a 73 per cent chance that p is something other than 0.3
blocks.answer:
The first line is right. The second line broke. L(0.3) is the probability of 3 in 10 if p were 0.3. It is not the probability that p is 0.3.

The third line inherits the error. Add the likelihoods at 0.1, 0.2, up to 0.9 and they come to about 0.91. Add more values of p between them and the total grows past 1. They are not a distribution for p, so 1 minus one of them means nothing.

Why it looks reasonable: the number came from a probability formula, and it is a probability. It is a probability of the data. Reading it as “the probability of p” swaps the two sides of the bar in P(X = 3 | p). That is the transposed conditional of section 9.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague looks at Kiran’s 52 of 131 men and says:

The likelihood ratio between a share of 0.30 and a share of 0.50 is about 1. So these data cannot tell us whether the share is nearer a third or a half.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what the claim gets wrong and what it gets right.
blocks.answer:
Compute each value’s likelihood against the best-supported share, 52 ÷ 131 = 0.397.

0.3 divided by 0.397 = 0.75567
0.7 divided by 0.603 = 1.16086
52 times -0.12167 = -6.3268
79 times 0.06478 = 5.1176
-6.3268 plus 5.1176 = -1.2092
0.5 divided by 0.397 = 1.25945
0.5 divided by 0.603 = 0.82919
52 times 0.10018 = 5.2094
79 times -0.08134 = -6.4259
5.2094 plus -6.4259 = -1.2165

10−1.2092 is about 0.062, and 10−1.2165 is about 0.061. Each value has about one sixteenth of the best-supported value’s likelihood.

What the colleague gets right: the ratio of 0.30 to 0.50 is about 1.02. So the data do not favour either of those two over the other.

What the claim gets wrong: the data are not uninformative. Both values sit on opposite sides of the peak at 0.397, about equally far down. The data favour a share near 0.4 over either by about 16 to 1. A ratio of two values tells you only about those two.

What none of this establishes: the share among young Indian men. The likelihood is built on volunteers at one college, and treats their results as independent.
